short: Split, salted, and smoked herrings.
note: Herrings cured by splitting, salting, and smoking, traditionally eaten as part of a British breakfast.

short: Squid prepared as food.
note: A culinary name for squid. The word is borrowed from Italian, where calamari is the plural of calamaro.

short: The capital of Sabah, on northern Borneo.
note: Kota Kinabalu is the capital of the Malaysian state of Sabah on Borneo’s northwestern coast. It was formerly known as Jesselton.

short: A port city on Mindanao in the Philippines.
note: Zamboanga City occupies the southwestern tip of the Zamboanga Peninsula on Mindanao, in the southern Philippines. Its history includes a Spanish fort and long-standing maritime connections.

sources.label: Zamboanga City government · History of the city

short: The sea between northern Borneo and the Philippines.
note: A western Pacific sea bordered by Palawan, several central and southern Philippine islands, and northeastern Borneo.

short: A line from Kipling’s “Mandalay.”
note: Rudyard Kipling’s “Mandalay” (1890) gives voice to a former British soldier longing for Burma. Its refrain pictures the dawn thundering out of China across the bay.

short: Samuel Johnson, the English writer and lexicographer.
note: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) wrote poetry, criticism, and a major English dictionary. James Boswell records his comparison of life aboard ship with imprisonment, made worse by the possibility of drowning.

short: Tony Weller’s warning about widows in The Pickwick Papers.
note: In chapter 23 of Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers, Tony Weller warns his son Sam that a widow can outmaneuver many ordinary women. The exchange is written in Weller’s distinctive dialect.

sources.label: Charles Dickens · The Pickwick Papers, chapter 23

short: German: “Certainly, fool!”
note: Gewiss means certainly or assuredly; Narr means fool. Together the words form the blunt German reply “Certainly, fool!”

short: Bazaar Malay, a regional trade language.
note: Bazaar Malay is a simplified contact variety of Malay historically used as a common language among speakers of different languages in maritime Southeast Asia. Pasar means market or bazaar.

short: Possibly Somerset Maugham’s quip about English cooking.
note: Possibly the quip commonly attributed to W. Somerset Maugham that breakfast is the surest way to eat well in England. The British Council reproduces it under his name.

sources.label: British Council · The Great British Breakfast

short: A biblical image of a warhorse eager for battle.
note: Job 39:25 describes a spirited warhorse sensing battle at a distance and responding to the noise of trumpets, captains, and shouting.

short: The legendary ghost ship condemned to sail forever.
note: The Flying Dutchman is a phantom ship whose captain is condemned to endless voyaging. The maritime legend appears in Frederick Marryat’s The Phantom Ship (1839) and Richard Wagner’s opera.

short: An image from Anaïs Nin’s Seduction of the Minotaur.
note: In Anaïs Nin’s Seduction of the Minotaur, travel through unfamiliar places is paired with an inward map. The novel concludes her sequence Cities of the Interior.

sources.label: Anaïs Nin · Seduction of the Minotaur
Honey & Wax · first-edition Solar Barque catalogue

term: finger of God reaching out to Adam
short: Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam.
note: Michelangelo’s fresco on the Sistine Chapel ceiling depicts God extending his hand toward the reclining Adam. Their nearly touching fingers concentrate the image of life being bestowed.

short: The opening of Johnson’s The Vanity of Human Wishes.
note: Samuel Johnson’s The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749), modeled on Juvenal’s tenth satire, surveys the dangers and disappointments attached to desires for wealth, power, fame, and long life.

sources.label: Samuel Johnson · The Vanity of Human Wishes

short: Thoreau’s image of purposeless travel in Walden.
note: In the conclusion to Walden, Henry David Thoreau uses counting Zanzibar’s cats as an example of empty travel, then urges the reader toward self-exploration. Walden was published in 1854.

short: The myth of Prometheus bringing fire to humanity.
note: Prometheus steals fire for mortals in Greek myth. In Shakespeare’s Love’s Labor’s Lost, act 4, scene 3, Berowne praises women’s eyes as a source of that inspiring fire and of learning.

sources.label: William Shakespeare · Love’s Labor’s Lost IV.3

term: Life is a mystery as deep
short: Mary Mapes Dodge’s poem “The Two Mysteries.”
note: “The Two Mysteries,” by Mary Mapes Dodge, compares the uncertainty of death with the equally mysterious nature of life. It offers consolation without claiming knowledge of the dead’s experience.

sources.label: St. Nicholas · memorial of Mary Mapes Dodge
The Carrier Dove, 1888 · text of The Two Mysteries

term: It may be you wait your time, Beast
short: Kipling’s “The Undertaker’s Horse.”
note: Rudyard Kipling’s poem addresses a horse used by an undertaker. Its speaker imagines his own funeral and the animal’s eventual death, giving the familiar horse an unsettling association with mortality.

short: Speaking several languages.
note: Able to speak or use several languages; also used of a group or text containing several languages.

short: Malay: my room or cabin.
note: Kamar means a room or cabin; the possessive ending -ku means my.

sources.label: A Malay Manual: vocabulary and possessive pronouns
